Messages.Author: brandonsantacruz
Messages.Body:
Under 5.1 of the tournament rules "Cheating"

"Cheating includes, but is not limited to, the following intentional
activities:

* Receiving outside assistance or coaching
* Looking at opponents' card faces while shuffling or cutting
their decks
* Collusion to alter the results of a game
* Misrepresenting rules or card texts or errata
* Using marked cards/sleeves (see section 4.6)
* Drawing extra cards
* Manipulating which cards are drawn from your deck or from an
opponent's deck
* Stalling to take advantage of a time limit
* Misrepresenting or obscuring public information (pool totals,
number of cards in deck, and so on)"

One thing that seems to come up in tournaments is where you will be
approaching the 2 hour mark and someone or some group of players in
the game will try to say you have to play fast, presumably so that
they have time to win. At times like this, is it appropriate to say,
"if you didn't want to run out of time, you should have played faster
earlier in the game," and play as normal, or is there some obligation
to hustle through my turn? What exactly is considered stalling?

I think that stalling is partly about what you do and partly what
you're thinking when you do it. It can take people a while to figure
out what they should do, but this isn't stalling because the intent is
to play the game properly. Trying to see if there's part of the game
they're not aware of(and being rushed into) could take a while.
Deciding on what you need to play during a master phase, discard, etc
is important, especially when you're down to the end game.

When you are in a winning position, or at least looking to pick up
that 1/2 vp, why feel pressured to make someone's game easier? Short
of having turn time limits, I don't see the "stalling" provision as
being that enforceable.

Brandon

> "if you didn't want to run out of time, you should have played faster
> earlier in the game," and play as normal, or is there some obligation
> to hustle through my turn? What exactly is considered stalling?

Well, to be fair, most of the time that someone is slow in the end of
the game, that same person has been slow the whole game. And if
someone is near ousting their prey, and excessively slow play is
likely to prevent that, it seems reasonable to ask people to play
faster. 'Cause they probably have been asking these people to play
faster the whole game already anyway.

I've very rarely been in a game where someone played at a reasonable
rate, and then suddenly got slow near the end of the time limit. I've
been in *plenty* of games where someone played slow, and then
continued to play slow near the end of the time limit. So saying "if

you didn't want to run out of time, you should have played faster

earlier in the game" is likely to get someone pissed off at you if
they are complaining that you are playing slowly. As if they are
complaining about you playing slowly at the end of the game, you were
probably playing slowly earlier in the game.

-Peter

Messages.Author: Aaron Clark
Messages.Body:


Colluding refers to an agreement made by players outside the game to
work together to achieve a particular result for a game or
tournament. An example of collusion might be a group of players
deciding to try to help one of their number to win a tournament so
that all of them can split the prize. Collusion does not refer to
alliances openly made between players during the course of a game.

As for the OP, I think I have experienced stalling tactics before, but
it is awfully hard to prove. Beware of players trying to hold
pointless political debates during the last forty minutes of a game,
that's all I have to say.

In my experience I have often tried to calculate my way to victory.
When all I have to rely on is myself I have to be sure the actions I
take are going to be the best actions and in the right order. I missed
my 2nd prey at last year's Origins final table (first major tourney
event) because I failed to play a certain stealth card as opposed to
another which mattered given the disciplines on my vampires taking the
actions and the one more card it would have moved (conditioning) and
would have thus obtained my oust and likely won the day. Due to this
event I made sure that in future tournaments I would not make this
mistake and at times take longer on my turn as it could effect the
game and I would rather not lose a game because I did not take time to
do the math. And I will get chastised at times as if I take too long,
and some could interpret this to be stalling. Yet I know this not to
be true as if it ever happens that I am taking my time on a turn, it
is too figure out how I survive or achieve my GW. Part of my success
it due to just that.

And on the flip side I have seen some of the world's top players
intentionally stall and they will openly admit it afterwards or admit
that they do stall games if it means the game win. To me that is total
BS and you should be a better player than that. The ironic thing is I
see those same players try to rush others and remind them of the time
on the clock if they think they have the GW in hand if enough turns go
by. Karma comes to mind. And to those that intentionally stall out
games I say you are cheating and perhaps stalling should be taken more
seriously by judges.

Messages.Author: Jeff Poole
Messages.Body:
On May 10, 2:45 pm, brandonsantacruz <brandonsantac...@yahoo.com>
wrote:

I think this is one of the slippery slopes of judging VtES (much like
playing to win) as it is almost total undefinable. Should a player be
given a set time per turn, a set time per turn per minute, no
restriction, should slow players be chastised on turn 1, should all
players take the same amount of time to consider decisions/
alternatives/deals, should bad play be penalized, etc?

When I am judging, I feel like a player is entitled to take his/her
time on his/her turn. Whether this is minute 1 or minute 117. This
means that a player can make actions that will have 0 effect on the
outcome of the game even in their last turn. If you try to limit
these actions on minute 118 then you should enforce the same stringent
on minute 5 (ie, that hunt is a total waste of time and will not help
you win the game, announcing it and resolving effects is stalling!)
which is impossible to do.

I would say as a rule of thumb, that unless a player's actions/
thoughts/inaction can be verified to be stalling the game out, that
they should not be rushed through their final minutes of the game. In
fact, I find it to be rather poor sportsmanship to rush someone
through their last turns because you "want to win".

Jeff Poole

> lack of emoticons. Where are you on this, Peter?

Heh--I think Norm is being completely serious here, in the sense of
"If someone is wasting time through table talk, call a judge and ask
them to stop". The problem here is that the line between "wasting time
with table talk" and "legitimate play of the game" is a very gray one.

I have certainly been in games where someone spent every possible
opportunity to try and convince someone at the table to do things for
them, even though it was clear that:

A) All of these requests were mostly insane.

and

B) All of these requests were mostly ignored.

But the player just kept trying. Which made their (and everyone else's
turn) move slowly. And unsurprisingly, these games timed out (in at
least one that I can think of like this, I could have conceivably won
had time not run out). I don't think it is at all unreasonable to, in
a situation like this, as a judge to intervene, which I think is what
Norm was talking about.

The problem, again, is that what one person sees as "flagrantly
wasting time with insane table discussion", another sees as "playing
the table", and while the first is illegal, the second is permitted.

To be fair, most games of tournament VTES I play don't time out. And
most of the ones that *do* time out, time out as a result of a locked
down table (i.e. no one can really oust anyone due to table situation,
rather than slow play, and it just grinds along till time runs out).
But once and a while, I have been in a game that did time out and
clearly timed out due to slow play and inordinate amounts of table
talk. But again, these are very few and far between.

-Peter

On May 12, 9:46 am, XZealot <xzea...@cox.net> wrote:
> That person gets a judge involved to deal with Mr. Stallingpants.

Alas, Mr. Stallingpants is unfortunately named, because he doesn't
actually stall.

Try this example instead. You announce a political action. Before you
even get to the "as announced" window, your prey and predator get into
a thirty second debate about which one of them, if either, should DI
your action. No stalling involved.

Next, your prey needs to decide whether or not he needs to block this
action. Looking at his hand, he sees that he can only reliably block
one of your actions, and isn't sure if this is the one. After thirty
seconds, he decides not to block.

Next, your predator goes through the same process as your prey, again
taking thirty seconds.

Next, there's a thirty-second debate about whether or not to play
Delaying Tactics on your vote.

Next, there's a thirty-second debate about who, if anyone, should DI
your Voter Cap.

No stalling involved there, just honest debate. But all of that non-
stalling eats up your timer, even though you're not necessarily
involved in the debate.



> enforceable?

The judge can't be 2 places at once (or 4 or 5). Only one table in a
tournament can get the judge to adjudicate. The others just have to
wait (burning up more time) or deal with it themselves (burning up
more time). Unless you can either say "It's my turn and you are
wasting valuable time here is a rule that says you must respond to the
acting players request for a response, you must respond now" then you
will have players who see strategic value in burning up time to time a
table out. I have witnessed stalling in many forms, I have never
witnessed a judge handle the situation where the stalling was punished
in any significant way to deter it.

adjudicate, should get more help (or the organizer should see to it
that there are more judges available, as the case may be). And even
for the occasional overwhelming coincidence of situations, the judge

Sounds like a need for better judging or better judges.

If the judges aren't enforcing the rules, changing the rules isn't
much of a solution.

Messages.Author: Kushiel
Messages.Body:
On May 12, 2:17 pm, XZealot <xzea...@cox.net> wrote:
> How do you deal with the "static" or "white-noise" generated by other
> players during your turn that delays your action from resolving?

Like, if I'm attempting to resolve an action and another player keeps
talking at me?

If it's not a player with whom I'm having some kind of mechanical
interaction, I tell them that I'll talk to them after my action or
turn, as appropriate.

If it is a player with whom I'm having some kind of mechanical
interaction, and they're refusing to make a decision in lieu of
talking at me, I'll simply adopt a firm tone of voice and tersely
explain that I'm not going to change my mind. "The action has already
been declared. Do you block?" is an example I can recall using, which
hasn't ever failed to move the game along.

It may be that this technique is buttressed by the fact that I don't
do a ton of negotiating myself. It's entirely possible that such a
playstyle results in other players believing me to be less likely to
be swayed by negotiation, though I'm just speculating now (you'd have
to ask them).

It's also just possible that years of playing with Ira in Pittsburgh
is the reason I taught myself these techniques, now that I think of
it... ;)

John Eno

and this in conjunction with there being 5 players on the table, all
of whom don't want to be "left out of the deal making" cause the
rounds to time out. The difference between stalling and legitimate,
yet excessive, deal-making is often a matter of perspective. Having
your time right in front of you tends to put things into perspective
prior to the calling of the 1 hour mark, which is usually the first
clear indication to a player as to how much time has elapsed in the
round. You want players to police there own table so that each table
doesn't have to have it's own judge. Keeping it from decending into a
open "he's the table threat. No, he's the table threat, No, he's the
table threat" blabfest would be good for the game.

Has it been tried?

your control is nonsensical.

I suppose you could have a timer and pass it around as per [1.6.1.5],
but that would be tedious in the extreme. (To verify, try playing a
game where you just say "pass" at *all* the times you have the impulse
(and make a hot-potato to pass around to the next person in impulse
order, or to pass back to "A" whenever any activity occurs).

Let me know how your tests go.

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
XZealot <xze...@cox.net> wrote:
>Player interaction with the player who's turn it is is valuable. Two
>players who's turn it is not working out a deal is not.

That second sentence is crap, I'm afraid.

When you call a Parity Shift that may well cause you to roll the table,
me discussing with another player how to stop that is valuable. When
that player wants to try to block, but wonders if he can borrow my Rumor
Mill to get the intercept? That's valuable. The player asking me pre-
emptively if he can't block, whether we can do anything about the
referendum and whether it might be worth him saving his block for the
next action instead? That's valuable. The cross-table player saying
"Errr... I can Sudden that master card for you. What's it worth?"
That's valuable. The player with an Eagle's Sight in hand saying "Don't
waste your wakes on that if you don't want to, Masika can give it a go
if you'll rescue me from torpor." That's valuable. The whole table
saying "OH CRAP" when it sees a deck pulling repeated Baltimore Purge or
a turbo-X deck, and working out who can block you or rush you or banish
you, with several people discussing this on anyone's turn? That's
valuable. Working out how to gang up on the Nergal deck in the infernal
storyline? That's valuable.

These are all perfectly reasonable plays, within both the rules and
spirit of the game. Ad hoc discussions of short-term and medium-term
goals are a perfectly ordinary facet of the game.

--
James Coupe

These are good specific examples of game play that pushes the game's
length.

Not because they are pithy one-liners, but rather once the cross table
action starts in a game the whole game slows down. Instead of the
impulse going back and forth between the acting player and the target
of his action. Each action must pause to pass the impulse to the
players not affected by the current action. The eagle sight is
example is a good one (as well as when Anneke hits the table). Do you
block? The targeted player or predator/prey of the acting player in
question have the impulse passed to them to block. Now there is
another player added to the mix which increases the time taken to
accept or decline blocks by at least 50% if you keep everything else
equal. All this adds time to a normally routine play. On top of that
you add, the associated haggling, bartering and other associated horse-
trading, and you have extended the time taken to play the game
considerably.

> These are all perfectly reasonable plays, within both the rules and
> spirit of the game.  Ad hoc discussions of short-term and medium-term
> goals are a perfectly ordinary facet of the game.

If they were limited to pithy phrase that looked like lines out of a
dr suess book then it would add a negligible time to the game. It is
when the haggling and bartering between 3 or more players (such as who
can make me the best offer?) that it really drags the game out.

I am looking for a solution to an apparent problem. If you don't
think it is a problem then no solution is required.
